title: Morning Sunlight Exposure
description: Expose your eyes to natural sunlight within the first 30 minutes of waking up to align your circadian rhythm, enhance mood, and improve alertness.
source: Huberman Lab, Business Insider, official Huberman YouTube

actions.action: Get at least 1000 lux of natural light exposure (ideally sunlight)
actions.duration: 5–10 minutes on sunny days; 10–20 minutes on cloudy days
actions.timing: Within the first 30–60 minutes of waking
actions.details: Go outside without sunglasses (contact lenses or prescription glasses are fine). Light through windows is not sufficient unless exceptionally bright. Avoid direct sunlight into the eyes—look toward the direction of sunlight, not at it.

benefits: Improves sleep quality by anchoring circadian rhythm
Boosts mood by increasing dopamine and serotonin levels
Enhances alertness and wakefulness in the morning
Supports healthy cortisol rhythm
May reduce risk of depression and seasonal affective disorder
science: Morning sunlight exposure stimulates intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs), which signal the brain's circadian clock (SCN) to regulate sleep, mood, and alertness. Exposure to 1000+ lux light in the morning leads to earlier melatonin offset and improved nighttime sleep (Huberman Lab Podcast).

title: Caffeine Delay (90-120 Min After Waking)
description: Delay your first caffeine intake to 90-120 minutes after waking to allow natural cortisol-driven alertness to peak, then use caffeine to extend focus without an afternoon crash.

actions.details: Resist coffee or tea immediately upon waking. Allow your natural cortisol awakening response (CAR) to peak first. Drink water and get morning sunlight instead. Then have your first caffeine at the 90-120 minute mark.

actions.action: Stop caffeine intake by early afternoon
actions.timing: No caffeine after ~2 PM (8-10 hours before bed)
actions.details: Caffeine has a half-life of 5-6 hours. To protect sleep architecture, avoid caffeine in the second half of the day. This pairs with the delay to give you a focused caffeine window.

benefits: Eliminates the mid-morning energy crash
Leverages natural cortisol for initial wakefulness
Extends afternoon focus and productivity
Improves sleep quality by reducing residual caffeine at night
Reduces caffeine dependency over time
science: Cortisol peaks naturally 30-45 minutes after waking (the Cortisol Awakening Response). Consuming caffeine during this peak blocks adenosine receptors while cortisol is already handling alertness, leading to a crash when cortisol drops. Delaying caffeine allows cortisol to do its job, then caffeine extends alertness afterward.
contraindications: May be difficult for those with strong caffeine habits — taper gradually
Not applicable if you don't consume caffeine

title: Daily Breathwork Protocol by Dr. Andrew Huberman
description: A science-backed breathing routine to optimize mental and physical health, reduce stress, and improve focus.

actions.details: Inhale deeply through the nose, then perform a second quick inhale followed by a long exhale through the mouth. Repeat this cycle for five minutes to activate the parasympathetic nervous system and reduce stress.

benefits: Reduces anxiety
Improves mood
Enhances sleep quality
Regulates autonomic nervous system
science: Cyclic sighing has been shown to be highly effective for reducing stress and improving sleep quality. It involves performing a series of physiological sighs continuously for a set period, which has been reported to improve mood, reduce anxiety, and enhance autonomic functions related to sleep and heart rate variability.
contraindications: Individuals with respiratory conditions should consult a healthcare provider before starting any new breathing exercises.

title: Evening Light Minimization
description: Minimize bright artificial light exposure between 10 PM and 4 AM to protect melatonin secretion, support circadian health, and improve sleep quality.

actions.action: Dim overhead lights and use low-positioned lamps after sunset
actions.details: Switch from overhead/ceiling lights to desk lamps, candles, or floor-level lighting. Light from above (like ceiling fixtures) more closely mimics sunlight and suppresses melatonin more than light from below eye level. Use warm-toned (amber/red) bulbs.

actions.action: Use blue-light blocking or night mode on screens
actions.details: Enable Night Shift/Night Light on devices or use blue-light blocking glasses. Reduce screen brightness. Better yet, minimize screen time in the last 1-2 hours before bed entirely.

benefits: Protects melatonin production for healthy sleep onset
Reduces cortisol dysregulation from nighttime light
Improves sleep latency (time to fall asleep)
Supports overall circadian rhythm health
Reduces risk of mood disruption from late-night light
science: Huberman emphasizes that bright light exposure between 10 PM and 4 AM suppresses dopamine, disrupts cortisol rhythm, and inhibits melatonin release via the habenula pathway. Even brief bright light at night can shift the circadian clock. The position of light matters — overhead light is more suppressive than light at or below eye level.
contraindications: None — universally safe and beneficial
Those with night-shift jobs should consult specialized circadian protocols

title: Hydration & Electrolyte Protocol
description: Optimize daily hydration with water and electrolytes (sodium, potassium, magnesium) to support brain function, physical performance, and energy levels throughout the day.

actions.action: Drink water with electrolytes upon waking
actions.details: Drink 16-32 oz (500-1000ml) of water with a pinch of sea salt (or electrolyte mix) first thing in the morning. You lose significant water during sleep through respiration and perspiration. Rehydrating quickly improves alertness and cognitive function.

Aim for roughly half your body weight in ounces of water per day (e.g., 160 lbs = ~80 oz). Ensure adequate electrolytes: sodium, potassium, and magnesium. Low-sugar electrolyte mixes or simply adding a pinch of salt and squeeze of lemon to water works well.

benefits: Improves cognitive function and focus
Supports physical performance and endurance
Prevents headaches and fatigue from dehydration
Supports kidney function and detoxification
Improves mood and energy levels
Essential for thermoregulation
science: Even mild dehydration (1-2% body water loss) impairs cognitive function, mood, and physical performance. Huberman emphasizes that water alone without electrolytes can dilute blood sodium, reducing the effectiveness of hydration. Sodium, potassium, and magnesium are essential for neuronal firing, muscle contraction, and fluid balance.
contraindications: Those with kidney disease should consult a physician about fluid and electrolyte intake
Excessive water without electrolytes can cause hyponatremia
Adjust intake based on activity level, climate, and body size

title: Pre-Bed Wind-Down Activities Protocol
description: Science-backed wind-down routine to prepare your body and mind for sleep by establishing consistent pre-bedtime activities that signal the transition to rest.
source: Huberman Lab AI - Matt Walker & Andrew Huberman

actions.details: Spend 10-15 minutes meditating to calm your mind. Focus on deep breathing, body scan, or mindfulness techniques. This helps activate the parasympathetic nervous system and reduce mental chatter.

actions.timing: After meditation or as standalone activity
actions.details: Engage in gentle stretching to release tension in your body. Focus on areas that hold stress like neck, shoulders, and lower back. Avoid vigorous stretching that might be too stimulating.
Choose a book or material that isn't too stimulating. Avoid screens to reduce blue light exposure. Select calming, non-thrilling content that won't activate your nervous system.
Listen to calming podcasts, nature sounds, or soft music. Avoid video content which can be too activating. Choose audio that promotes relaxation and mental calm.
A warm bath or shower helps relax muscles and signals to your body that it's time to wind down. The temperature change can also help with the natural drop in body temperature needed for sleep.

Instead of counting sheep, imagine a familiar walk in intricate detail. Visualize every step, sound, and sensation to distract your mind and ease you into sleep. This technique helps quiet mental chatter.

benefits: Signals to your body that it's time to prepare for sleep
Activates parasympathetic nervous system for relaxation
Reduces mental chatter and racing thoughts
Helps establish consistent sleep-wake rhythm
Releases physical tension and muscle stress
Creates psychological association between activities and sleep
Reduces blue light exposure before bed
science: Wind-down routines help signal to your body that it's time to prepare for sleep, making the transition smoother - akin to decelerating a vehicle before stopping. Consistent activities create psychological associations that prime the nervous system for rest. Meditation activates the parasympathetic nervous system, while gentle stretching releases physical tension. Avoiding stimulating content prevents activation of the sympathetic nervous system that would interfere with sleep onset.
contraindications: Avoid vigorous exercise or stimulating activities
Don't engage in work-related or stressful conversations
Avoid bright screens and blue light exposure
Skip caffeine or other stimulants during wind-down time
Don't choose reading material that's too exciting or anxiety-provoking

title: Optic Flow Walking
description: Deliberate forward walking outdoors — without headphones — to generate optic flow, which suppresses amygdala activity and reduces anxiety and stress at a neurological level.

actions.timing: Any time of day — morning or post-work ideal
actions.details: Walk outdoors at a comfortable pace in a forward direction. The key is self-generated forward motion — not a treadmill, bike, or car. Leave headphones behind. Allow your eyes to naturally take in the passing visual environment (optic flow). This is not an exercise protocol — the goal is visual stimulation suppressing the amygdala, not cardiovascular output.

Soften your gaze and allow your visual field to expand to peripheral vision. Don't fix your eyes on a single point — let the environment pass. This wide-angle, forward-motion visual input is the active ingredient in optic flow's anxiety-reducing effect.

benefits: Reduces amygdala activity and acute anxiety
Lowers cortisol and sympathetic nervous system tone
Improves mood through visual stimulation of brainstem circuits
Accessible — requires no equipment or cost
Stacks with morning sunlight and outdoor distance viewing
Supports processing of stressful events
science: Forward self-generated locomotion creates optic flow — the visual impression of the environment streaming past. Research shows this specific visual pattern suppresses activity in the amygdala (the brain's threat-detection center), reducing fear and anxiety states. The mechanism is distinct from exercise-induced mood effects. Huberman cites this as one of the most underused and accessible mental health tools available.
contraindications: Treadmill walking does not produce the same optic flow effect
Headphone use (especially audio that demands attention) blunts the visual engagement

title: Ultradian Work Cycles (90-Minute Focus Blocks)
description: Structure deep work into 90-minute blocks aligned with the brain's natural ultradian rhythm, followed by genuine rest, to maximize focus and prevent cognitive fatigue.
duration: 90 minutes of focused work + 10-20 min break

actions.details: Set a timer for 90 minutes and work on a single task or project with minimal distractions. It's normal for the first 5-10 minutes to feel unfocused — this is the ramp-up phase. True deep focus typically engages around 10-20 minutes in. Resist checking phone or email during the block.

actions.action: Take a genuine rest break between blocks
actions.details: Step away from screens. Walk, look at a distance, do light stretching, or practice NSDR. Avoid switching to another cognitively demanding task or scrolling social media, which does not constitute rest for the prefrontal cortex.

benefits: Aligns work with the brain's natural 90-minute attention cycles
Maximizes depth and quality of focus
Prevents cognitive fatigue and burnout
Improves output per hour of work
Creates clear boundaries between work and rest
science: The brain operates in ~90-minute ultradian cycles of higher and lower alertness throughout the day (the same rhythm seen in sleep cycles). Huberman explains that working in alignment with these cycles allows for deeper engagement of prefrontal cortex circuits. Forcing focus beyond 90 minutes yields diminishing returns and increases errors.
contraindications: May not be practical for jobs requiring constant reactivity (e.g., customer support)
Not every task requires a full 90-minute block — adapt as needed

title: Cardiovascular Exercise Protocol
description: A science-backed aerobic exercise routine to enhance cardiovascular health, improve endurance, and support overall physical performance.

actions.details: Engage in moderate-intensity aerobic exercise such as brisk walking, jogging, cycling, or swimming. Maintain a heart rate within 50–70% of your maximum heart rate.

actions.timing: after moderate-intensity sessions or on separate days
actions.details: Incorporate intervals of high-intensity cardio (e.g., sprints or fast cycling) followed by rest periods to improve cardiovascular capacity and VO2 max.

benefits: Improves heart health and circulation
Increases endurance and aerobic capacity
Supports weight management
Enhances mood and reduces stress
science: Aerobic exercise has been extensively studied and shown to improve cardiovascular function, enhance mitochondrial efficiency, reduce blood pressure, and support overall longevity. High-intensity interval training can further boost VO2 max and cardiovascular performance.
contraindications: Individuals with cardiovascular or respiratory conditions should consult a healthcare provider before starting this protocol.
Not recommended for those with acute injuries without clearance from a professional.

title: Strength Training Protocol
description: A science-backed resistance training routine to build muscle strength, size, and overall physical performance.

actions.details: Perform compound lifts such as squats, deadlifts, bench press, rows, and overhead presses. Include 3–4 sets of 6–12 reps for each major muscle group. Rest 60–90 seconds between sets.
Add isolation exercises for smaller muscle groups (biceps, triceps, calves, abs) to support balanced muscle development.

benefits: Increases muscular strength and endurance
Promotes hypertrophy and muscle mass growth
Improves bone density
Enhances overall functional fitness
science: Strength training stimulates muscle protein synthesis and promotes neuromuscular adaptations. Regular resistance training improves muscle strength, endurance, bone health, and metabolic efficiency.
contraindications: Individuals with acute injuries or musculoskeletal limitations should consult a healthcare provider before starting.
Improper technique can lead to injury; proper form and progression are essential.

title: Vision Breaks for Eye Health
description: Regular breaks from close-up work to prevent eye strain, reduce fatigue, and maintain visual health through the 20-20-20 rule and deliberate blinking.
source: Huberman Lab, Healthline, Huberman Lab Newsletter

actions.details: Every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away for at least 20 seconds. Set a timer or use an app reminder to maintain consistency.

actions.frequency: Every few minutes during screen time
actions.details: Slow, deliberate blinks help rewet the eyes. Close your eyes completely for a full second with each blink.

benefits: Reduces digital eye strain and computer vision syndrome
Prevents dry eyes and maintains natural tear film
Reduces risk of myopia progression
Improves focus flexibility and accommodation
Decreases headaches and eye fatigue
Maintains healthy blinking patterns
science: The 20-20-20 rule helps relax the ciliary muscles responsible for focusing, preventing accommodative spasm. Regular distance viewing stimulates parasympathetic nervous system activity, promoting eye muscle relaxation. Deliberate blinking maintains the tear film layer essential for eye health and clear vision.
contraindications: None - safe for all ages and visual conditions

title: Afternoon Sunlight Viewing
description: View sunlight in the late afternoon to signal your circadian clock that evening is approaching, which helps protect against the negative effects of artificial light at night on melatonin production.

actions.action: View low solar angle sunlight in the late afternoon
actions.timing: Late afternoon, ideally in the last 1-2 hours before sunset
actions.details: Go outside and look toward the sun (not directly at it) as it descends. The yellow-orange light at low solar angles activates a different set of retinal neurons that signal 'evening' to your circadian clock. This provides a second anchor point for your internal clock.

benefits: Provides a second circadian anchor point (complementing morning light)
Reduces sensitivity to artificial light at night
Protects melatonin onset from being delayed by evening screen use
Supports consistent sleep-wake timing
Free and requires no equipment
science: Afternoon/evening sunlight exposure at low solar angles activates melanopsin-containing retinal ganglion cells in a pattern that signals 'dusk' to the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN). Huberman explains this acts as a protective buffer — it reduces the melatonin-suppressing effect of artificial light exposure later in the evening by up to 50%.
contraindications: Do not stare directly at the sun
Use UV protection if extended exposure in bright conditions

title: Deliberate Cold Exposure
description: Deliberate cold water immersion to boost dopamine, norepinephrine, and resilience. Huberman recommends 11 minutes total per week across 2-4 sessions for lasting neurochemical benefits.

actions.action: Cold water immersion (cold shower, ice bath, or cold plunge)
actions.timing: Morning preferred for maximum dopamine & alertness benefit
actions.details: Enter water cold enough to make you want to get out but safe to stay in (typically 45-60°F / 7-15°C). Submerge up to the neck. Control your breathing with slow exhales. End the session on cold — do not warm up with a hot shower immediately, as shivering extends the metabolic benefit.
Allow your body to rewarm naturally through shivering and movement. This extends the dopamine and norepinephrine elevation. Avoid jumping into a hot shower right away.

benefits: Increases dopamine by 200-300% for several hours
Boosts norepinephrine for alertness and focus
Builds mental resilience and stress tolerance
Improves mood and reduces symptoms of depression
Enhances brown fat thermogenesis and metabolism
Reduces inflammation and supports recovery
science: Cold exposure triggers a massive release of norepinephrine (200-300%) and dopamine (250%) from the locus coeruleus and adrenal glands. Unlike stimulant-based dopamine spikes, cold-induced dopamine elevation is long-lasting (hours). The practice also increases brown adipose tissue activity, improving metabolic health over time.
contraindications: Individuals with cardiovascular conditions (Raynaud's, heart disease) should consult a physician
Never do cold water immersion alone — drowning risk exists
Avoid immediately after strength training if hypertrophy is the goal (blunts adaptation)
Start conservatively — hypothermia is a real risk at extreme temperatures

title: Nasal Breathing Practice
description: Deliberately practice nasal breathing during the day and especially during low-to-moderate exercise to improve oxygen delivery, filter air, and activate the parasympathetic nervous system.

actions.action: Breathe through your nose during daily activities and exercise
actions.timing: Throughout the day, especially during low-moderate intensity exercise
actions.details: Consciously close your mouth and breathe through your nose during walking, working, and exercising at low to moderate intensity. Nasal breathing produces nitric oxide, which dilates blood vessels and improves oxygen delivery. During high-intensity exercise, mouth breathing is acceptable when needed.

Use medical-grade mouth tape to encourage nasal breathing during sleep. Start with a small strip and ensure you can breathe freely through your nose before attempting. This reduces snoring and improves sleep quality. Discontinue if uncomfortable.

benefits: Increases nitric oxide production for better oxygen delivery
Filters, warms, and humidifies incoming air
Activates parasympathetic nervous system (calming)
Reduces over-breathing and CO2 loss
Improves exercise efficiency at submaximal intensities
May reduce snoring and improve sleep quality
science: Nasal breathing produces nitric oxide in the paranasal sinuses, which acts as a vasodilator improving oxygen uptake by 10-15%. Huberman discusses how nasal breathing preferentially activates the parasympathetic nervous system compared to mouth breathing, which tends to activate sympathetic (stress) pathways. The nasal passages also filter pathogens and warm incoming air.
contraindications: Nasal congestion or deviated septum may require medical treatment first
Do not force nasal breathing during high-intensity exercise if it causes distress
Mouth taping is not suitable for those with nasal obstruction, sleep apnea, or nasal polyps

title: Focus Meditation (13-Minute Daily)
description: A daily 13-minute meditation practice focused on sustained attention to a single point (breath, visual target, or body sensation) to improve focus, attention span, and memory.

actions.timing: Any consistent time of day (morning recommended)
actions.details: Sit comfortably and focus your attention on a single point — your breath, a visual target (like a candle flame or spot on the wall), or an internal body sensation. When your mind wanders, gently return focus to the target. The act of refocusing IS the exercise that builds attentional circuits. Don't aim for perfect focus; aim for consistent refocusing.

benefits: Improves sustained attention and focus within 8 weeks
Enhances working memory capacity
Reduces default mode network activity (mind wandering)
Increases prefrontal cortex function
Supports emotional regulation
Accessible to beginners with no prior meditation experience
science: A study from Wendy Suzuki's lab (discussed on Huberman Lab) found that 13 minutes of daily focused attention meditation for 8 weeks significantly improved attention, mood, and memory. The key mechanism is the repeated act of refocusing attention, which strengthens prefrontal cortex circuits involved in top-down attentional control.
contraindications: None for most people
If meditation increases anxiety, start with shorter sessions (5 minutes) and build up

title: NSDR After Poor Sleep
description: Non-Sleep Deep Rest (NSDR) protocols to restore alertness and cognitive function after poor sleep, using guided relaxation techniques to reset the nervous system.
source: Huberman Lab Podcast, Sleep Foundation research

conditional.question: Did you sleep poorly last night?

actions.details: Use a guided Yoga Nidra or NSDR protocol. Lie down comfortably and follow breathing and body scan instructions to achieve deep relaxation without sleep.
Systematically tense and release muscle groups throughout the body while focusing on the contrast between tension and relaxation.

benefits: Restores alertness and cognitive function after poor sleep
Reduces stress and anxiety from sleep deprivation
Activates parasympathetic nervous system for recovery
Improves mood and emotional regulation
Can partially compensate for lost REM sleep benefits
Reduces cortisol levels and stress response
science: NSDR protocols activate the parasympathetic nervous system and can restore dopamine levels in the brain. Studies show that Yoga Nidra increases dopamine in the basal forebrain by up to 65%, helping compensate for the dopamine depletion that occurs after poor sleep.
contraindications: Should not replace regular sleep
Avoid if experiencing severe insomnia without medical consultation

title: Dopamine Management Protocol
description: Manage dopamine peaks and troughs deliberately to sustain motivation, avoid burnout, and maintain a healthy baseline. Avoid layering too many dopamine-triggering behaviors simultaneously.

actions.details: Do not combine multiple high-dopamine activities simultaneously (e.g., music + pre-workout + caffeine + phone scrolling before a workout). Stacking amplifies the peak but deepens the subsequent trough, reducing baseline dopamine over time.
Randomly celebrate wins rather than rewarding every accomplishment. This mimics a variable reinforcement schedule, which sustains dopamine release and motivation better than constant rewards.
Avoid high-stimulation, low-effort dopamine sources (social media, news scrolling, video games) during focused work blocks and the first/last hour of the day.

benefits: Maintains healthy dopamine baseline for sustained motivation
Prevents burnout and anhedonia from dopamine depletion
Improves ability to find satisfaction in effort-based activities
Reduces phone/social media dependency
Enhances focus and goal-directed behavior
science: Dopamine operates on a trough-peak system: large peaks are followed by proportional troughs below baseline. Repeated high-dopamine stimulation without recovery lowers the baseline, leading to reduced motivation and pleasure (anhedonia). Intermittent reinforcement and avoiding dopamine stacking help maintain a healthy set point.
contraindications: Not a substitute for treatment of clinical depression or ADHD
Excessive restriction of all pleasurable activities is not the goal

title: Heart Rate Variability (HRV) Improvement Protocol
description: Science-backed protocol to enhance Heart Rate Variability (HRV) through breathing techniques, music therapy, and nutrition to improve autonomic nervous system balance and recovery.
source: Huberman Lab AI - Andy Galpin & Andrew Huberman

actions.details: Practice breathing techniques emphasizing extended exhales. Inhale for 4 counts, exhale for 6-8 counts. This helps lower heart rate and promotes calmness by activating the parasympathetic nervous system.

actions.timing: During stress or as daily practice
actions.details: Inhale for 4 counts, hold for 4 counts, exhale for 4 counts, hold for 4 counts. Repeat this cycle to enhance HRV and manage stress effectively.

actions.timing: During moments of stress or anxiety
actions.details: Perform double inhales through the nose followed by a long exhale through the mouth. This technique is highly effective for managing stress and improving HRV.
Listen to calming music for 10-30 minutes daily. Choose music that promotes relaxation and engages the parasympathetic nervous system to boost HRV and physiological resilience.
Ensure adequate omega-3 fatty acid intake through diet or supplementation. Omega-3s are associated with improved HRV, enhanced mood, and reduced anxiety symptoms.

Use a reliable HRV monitoring device to track your progress. Note that device accuracy varies, so focus on trends rather than absolute values. Higher HRV indicates better autonomic nervous system balance.

benefits: Improves autonomic nervous system balance
Enhances recovery from stress and exercise
Increases vagal tone and parasympathetic activity
Reduces overall stress and anxiety levels
Promotes better emotional regulation
Supports cardiovascular health
Enhances physiological resilience and adaptability
science: HRV refers to the variation in time between heartbeats, serving as an indicator of autonomic nervous system function. Higher HRV indicates healthy balance between sympathetic (fight or flight) and parasympathetic (rest and digest) states. Irregular heartbeats (greater HRV) correlate with states of rest and recovery, while rhythmic patterns (lower HRV) suggest stress. Vagal tone, associated with the vagus nerve, influences HRV and plays a role in regulating heart rate and emotional states. Breathing techniques with extended exhales help lower heart rate and promote calmness by activating the parasympathetic nervous system.
contraindications: Be cautious with HRV devices - not all are reliable and comparisons between individuals can be misleading
If you have cardiovascular conditions, consult a healthcare provider before starting breathing exercises
Start slowly with breathing techniques if you're new to them
Omega-3 supplements may interact with blood-thinning medications - consult your doctor

title: Omega-3 / EPA Supplementation
description: Daily supplementation with omega-3 fatty acids (targeting 1-2g EPA) to support mood, cardiovascular health, brain function, and reduce inflammation.

actions.action: Take omega-3 supplement with at least 1g EPA
actions.timing: With a meal containing fat for better absorption
actions.details: Take a high-quality fish oil, krill oil, or algae-based omega-3 supplement. The key metric is EPA content — aim for at least 1000mg (1g) EPA per day. EPA (not DHA) is the primary driver of the mood and anti-inflammatory benefits. Check the label for EPA specifically.

benefits: Significant antidepressant effects at 1g+ EPA/day
Reduces systemic inflammation
Supports cardiovascular health
Improves brain function and neuronal membrane fluidity
May improve HRV (heart rate variability)
Supports joint health and recovery
science: Huberman cites meta-analyses showing that EPA at doses of 1-2g/day has antidepressant effects comparable to some prescription medications. EPA modulates the inflammatory pathway by competing with arachidonic acid, reducing pro-inflammatory eicosanoid production. The mood effect is primarily from EPA, not DHA, though DHA supports brain structure.
contraindications: May interact with blood-thinning medications — consult physician
Some people experience fish burps — taking with meals or using enteric-coated capsules helps
High doses (>3g/day) may increase bleeding risk

title: Time-Restricted Eating (Intermittent Fasting)
description: Confine food intake to an 8-10 hour window each day, aligned with your circadian rhythm, to support metabolic health, reduce inflammation, and improve body composition.

actions.timing: Ideally starting 1-2 hours after waking, ending 2-3 hours before bed
actions.details: Choose a consistent eating window (e.g., 10 AM - 6 PM). Consume all meals and caloric beverages within this window. Water, black coffee, and plain tea are fine outside the window. Consistency of timing matters more than exact window length.
Late-night eating disrupts sleep architecture and shifts circadian clock gene expression in the liver. Finish your last meal at least 2-3 hours before bedtime.

benefits: Improves insulin sensitivity and blood glucose regulation
Supports healthy body composition and fat loss
Reduces systemic inflammation
Aligns peripheral clocks with circadian rhythm
May support longevity through autophagy activation
Improves digestive health
science: Time-restricted eating (TRE) aligns food intake with circadian biology. Satchin Panda's research (discussed extensively on Huberman Lab) shows TRE improves metabolic markers even without calorie reduction. Eating within a consistent window synchronizes liver, gut, and muscle clocks with the master clock in the SCN.
contraindications: Not recommended for individuals with eating disorders or history of disordered eating
Pregnant or breastfeeding women should not fast without medical supervision
Those on blood sugar medications should consult a physician
May not be suitable for high-performance athletes requiring frequent fueling

title: Gratitude Practice (Story-Based)
description: A neuroscience-backed gratitude practice that involves receiving or reading a genuine story of gratitude (not just listing things you're grateful for), which activates pro-social brain circuits and serotonin pathways.

actions.action: Read or recall a genuine story of gratitude
actions.details: Find or write a brief story about someone genuinely receiving help or expressing gratitude. It doesn't have to be YOUR story — observing genuine gratitude activates the same neural circuits. Re-read the same story if it still moves you. The key is emotional resonance, not novelty.

benefits: Activates pro-social prefrontal circuits
Increases serotonin and shifts autonomic tone toward calm
More effective than gratitude lists (which often feel performative)
Takes only 5 minutes for measurable neural effects
Improves resilience and subjective well-being
Effects are cumulative over weeks
science: Huberman explains that traditional gratitude lists are less effective because they can feel forced. The neuroscience shows that the most potent gratitude effect comes from the narrative experience of receiving or witnessing genuine gratitude. This activates the medial prefrontal cortex and anterior cingulate cortex — areas associated with empathy, reward, and pro-social behavior — and shifts autonomic nervous system function.
contraindications: None — safe for everyone
Those experiencing grief or loss should choose timing that feels appropriate

title: Expressive Journaling Protocol for Mental Health
description: A science-backed journaling method developed by Dr. James Pennebaker, shown to enhance emotional processing, reduce stress, and improve overall well-being.

actions.details: Write continuously about a significant emotional experience or trauma. Focus on expressing your deepest thoughts and feelings without concern for grammar or spelling.
Engage in calming activities such as deep breathing, meditation, or a short walk to help process emotions and stabilize mood.

benefits: Improves emotional processing
Reduces symptoms of anxiety and depression
Enhances immune function
Promotes neuroplasticity and brain rewiring

title: Foundational Fitness (Weekly Schedule)
description: Huberman's complete weekly fitness template combining cardiovascular training, resistance training, and flexibility work across a structured 5-6 day schedule for comprehensive fitness.

actions.details: Sustained low-to-moderate intensity cardio: jogging, cycling, rowing, or brisk hiking. Heart rate in Zone 2 (can hold a conversation but slightly breathless). Builds mitochondrial density and aerobic base.
Focus on quads, hamstrings, glutes, and calves. Exercises: squats, leg press, RDLs, lunges, calf raises. 3-4 sets of 5-8 reps for strength or 8-15 for hypertrophy.
Sauna, cold plunge, yoga, or light walking. Focus on recovery and mobility. This day supports the training days around it.
Chest, back, shoulders, and arms. Exercises: bench press, rows, overhead press, pull-ups, curls. Alternate push and pull movements. 3-4 sets of 6-12 reps.
Sprint intervals, rowing intervals, or cycling intervals. 30-60 seconds work, 30-90 seconds rest. This builds VO2 max and anaerobic capacity.

benefits: Addresses all components of fitness: endurance, strength, and flexibility
Structured for sustainable long-term adherence
Balances training stimulus with recovery
Adaptable to different fitness levels
Based on Huberman's personal training schedule
Combines cardiovascular and resistance training optimally

The weekly split allows adequate recovery between sessions while maintaining training frequency.

Avoid training through acute pain

description: Spend time outdoors looking at distant objects to support healthy eye development, reduce myopia risk, and provide natural light exposure for circadian health.

actions.details: Spend time outdoors looking at objects at least 20 feet away. Walk, sit in a park, or engage in outdoor activities while consciously viewing distant landscapes, trees, or horizon.

benefits: Reduces risk of myopia development and progression
Provides natural bright light exposure (2000+ lux)
Supports healthy circadian rhythm regulation

title: Sleep Support Supplements Protocol
description: Science-backed supplement stack to enhance sleep quality, reduce sleep latency, and support deeper restorative sleep through targeted neurotransmitter and mineral support.
source: Huberman Lab Newsletter - Toolkit for Sleep

actions.details: Take 145mg Magnesium Threonate OR 200mg Magnesium Bisglycinate, 50mg Apigenin, and 100-400mg Theanine. Start with one supplement and add others gradually as needed.

actions.action: Optional additional supplements (3-4 nights per week)
actions.details: Add 2g Glycine and 100mg GABA to the core stack. These can enhance sleep depth and reduce nighttime awakenings.
Track sleep quality and adjust dosages or combinations based on individual response. Some people may not need all supplements.

benefits: Reduces time to fall asleep (sleep latency)
Improves sleep quality and depth
Reduces nighttime awakenings
Supports natural melatonin production
Enhances GABA activity for relaxation
Provides magnesium for muscle relaxation and nervous system support

title: Worry Journal Protocol for Better Sleep
description: Science-backed journaling technique to reduce nighttime worries and improve sleep quality by writing down concerns earlier in the evening to clear mental clutter before bed.
source: Huberman Lab AI - Matt Walker & Andrew Huberman

actions.details: Write down all your worries, concerns, and thoughts in a dedicated journal. Include both specific problems and general anxieties. The goal is to 'close down all emotional tabs' in your mind, similar to shutting down a computer with too many active tabs.

For each worry, write down: 1) What you're worried about, 2) Why it's concerning you, 3) Any potential solutions or next steps, 4) Whether it's within your control. This structured approach helps organize thoughts and reduce mental chaos.

actions.timing: At the end of journaling session
actions.details: Close your journal and mentally acknowledge that you've addressed your worries for the day. Take a few deep breaths and consciously decide to set aside these concerns until tomorrow. This creates psychological closure.

Briefly review the previous night's worries to see which ones still feel important and which may have resolved themselves. This helps you recognize patterns and realize that many nighttime worries are amplified by fatigue.

benefits: Reduces time to fall asleep by up to 50%
Clears mental clutter and racing thoughts
Provides psychological closure on daily concerns
Reduces nighttime anxiety and worry amplification
Improves overall sleep quality and duration
Helps organize thoughts and prioritize concerns
Creates healthy separation between day and night mental states
science: According to Matt Walker, maintaining a worry journal helps 'close down all of the emotional tabs' in your mind, similar to shutting down a computer with too many active tabs that can impede sleep. Writing down worries earlier in the evening (not right before bed) helps clear your mind of nagging thoughts and concerns, making it easier to fall asleep. This practice has been shown to decrease the time it takes to fall asleep by 50%, comparable to some sleep medications. It counteracts the amplified anxiety that often occurs at night, leading to more manageable feelings during the day.
contraindications: Don't journal right before bed - allow 1-2 hours between journaling and sleep
Avoid dwelling on worries without structure - use the structured approach
Don't use this as a replacement for professional mental health care if needed
Avoid re-reading old worries excessively - focus on current concerns

title: High-Dose Creatine After Poor Sleep
description: On days following poor sleep, a significantly higher creatine dose (~0.35 g/kg body weight, or 20–25 g for most adults) can blunt sleep-deprivation-related cognitive decline. This is separate from your regular daily 5 g maintenance dose.
duration: Once, morning of a poor-sleep day
source: McMorris et al. 2024 (PMC); Huberman Lab; Dr. Rhonda Patrick

conditional.question: Did you sleep poorly last night?

actions.action: Take a high-dose creatine rescue dose
actions.timing: Morning, ideally within 1–2 hours of waking
actions.details: Take ~0.35 g per kg of body weight (roughly 20–25 g for a 70 kg person, or 15–20 g for a lighter individual). Mix into water, juice, or a smoothie in divided sips — do not take all at once to reduce GI discomfort. This is IN ADDITION to your regular 5 g daily dose.
Higher creatine doses require more water. Target at least 3 liters on days you take the rescue dose to prevent cramping or GI issues.

benefits: Shown to restore cognitive performance after sleep deprivation
Reduces reaction time slowing caused by poor sleep
Supports executive function, working memory, and attention
Addresses neuroenergetic deficit (ATP) in the prefrontal cortex after sleep loss
Used by Huberman and discussed extensively by Dr. Rhonda Patrick
science: A 2024 randomized trial (McMorris et al., PMC10902318) found that a single 0.35 g/kg creatine dose significantly improved cognitive performance in sleep-deprived subjects. Creatine raises cerebral phosphocreatine, which replenishes ATP rapidly in the prefrontal cortex — the area most impaired by sleep deprivation. Rhonda Patrick and Huberman Lab both highlight this as a practical acute intervention. Huberman has noted he raises his own intake to 10–15 g on poor-sleep days.
contraindications: Divide doses into 2–3 sips to minimize GI discomfort at high amounts
Not suitable for those with kidney disease — consult physician first
Do not exceed 30 g in a single day
Ensure adequate hydration

description: High-Intensity Interval Training to boost alertness, energy, and cognitive function after a night of poor sleep by increasing dopamine and adrenaline.

actions.details: Perform 30 seconds of high-intensity exercise (jumping jacks, burpees, sprint) followed by 30 seconds rest. Repeat 5-15 rounds depending on fitness level.
Rapidly climb stairs for 30-60 seconds, rest for 30 seconds, repeat. This provides similar benefits when gym equipment isn't available.

benefits: Rapidly increases alertness and energy levels
Boosts dopamine and adrenaline to combat fatigue
Improves cognitive function and focus
Enhances mood through endorphin release
Increases metabolic rate for sustained energy
Can partially offset negative effects of sleep loss
science: High-intensity exercise triggers release of dopamine, adrenaline, and BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor), which help compensate for the neurochemical imbalances caused by sleep deprivation. The stress response from HIIT can temporarily override fatigue signals.

title: Red Light / Photobiomodulation
description: Brief morning exposure to 670nm red light to recharge retinal mitochondria and slow age-related photoreceptor decline. Supported by research showing significant improvements in visual acuity in adults over 40.

actions.timing: Within the first 3 hours of waking
actions.details: Look toward a 670nm red light source (LED panel or red light device) from a distance of about 1-2 feet. Keep eyes open and relaxed — do not stare fixedly, blink naturally. 2-3 minutes is the studied dose. Do this in the morning only — evening red light exposure does not carry the same benefit and may interfere with sleep timing. Low-cost 670nm LED panels are widely available.

For muscle recovery and skin health, use a 650-850nm red/near-infrared panel at 1-2 feet distance for 10-15 minutes. This is a separate use case from the retinal protocol — different mechanism (skin and muscle mitochondria vs. photoreceptor mitochondria), different devices. Not required for the eye health benefit.

benefits: Counteracts age-related mitochondrial decline in retinal photoreceptors
Studies show 22% improvement in visual acuity in adults over 40
Reduces photoreceptor fatigue and improves color contrast sensitivity
Near-infrared wavelengths support muscle recovery and skin repair
Non-invasive and low-risk when used correctly
science: Retinal cone cells are among the most metabolically active cells in the body and rely heavily on mitochondrial function. Mitochondrial efficiency declines with age, leading to photoreceptor deterioration. Research published in the Journals of Gerontology (cited by Huberman) found that 3 minutes of 670nm light exposure in the morning 3x/week reversed some age-related visual decline. The mechanism is mitochondrial stimulation — red wavelengths are absorbed by cytochrome c oxidase, boosting ATP production in photoreceptors.
contraindications: Do not stare directly into high-intensity red light devices at close range
Those with photosensitive conditions (lupus, porphyria) should consult a physician
Evening use of bright red light panels may interfere with melatonin in some individuals
Not a replacement for regular eye exams

title: Studying & Learning (Self-Testing Protocol)
description: Use active recall and self-testing as the primary study method rather than passive re-reading, leveraging the testing effect to dramatically improve long-term retention and understanding.

actions.action: Test yourself on material rather than re-reading
actions.timing: During and after learning new material
actions.details: After reading or watching material, close the source and attempt to recall the key points from memory. Write them down or speak them aloud. The struggle of retrieval is what strengthens memory. Don't look at the material until you've attempted recall. Test yourself immediately after learning and then at spaced intervals.

actions.action: Use spaced repetition for long-term retention
actions.timing: Any time, but shortly after sleep is effective
actions.details: Review material at increasing intervals: 1 day, 3 days, 7 days, 14 days. Use flashcards (physical or apps like Anki) to automate spacing. Each retrieval attempt strengthens the neural pathway, making the memory more durable.

benefits: Dramatically improves long-term retention (testing effect)
More effective than re-reading or highlighting by 50-100%
Identifies knowledge gaps early
Strengthens neural pathways through effortful retrieval
Builds confidence through demonstrated knowledge
Works for any subject matter
science: Huberman discusses extensive research on the 'testing effect' — actively retrieving information strengthens memory far more than passive review. Each retrieval attempt triggers neuroplasticity in hippocampal and cortical circuits. The effort of recall (even when incorrect) signals the brain that this information is important, triggering consolidation during subsequent sleep.
contraindications: None — effective for all ages and subjects
May feel frustrating initially if accustomed to passive study — this is normal and part of the benefit

title: Stress Inoculation Protocol
description: Deliberately expose yourself to a controlled stressor (cold, HIIT, public speaking) while actively practicing cognitive calm during the adrenaline spike — training your prefrontal cortex to stay online under stress.

actions.timing: Morning or early day (not before bed)
actions.details: Select a stressor that reliably spikes adrenaline for you: cold water immersion (1-3 min at 55°F/13°C or colder), 5-10 minutes of high-intensity exercise, a difficult conversation, or brief public speaking. The stressor must feel genuinely uncomfortable — mild discomfort doesn't train the circuit.

actions.action: Maintain cognitive function during the stressor
actions.details: While in the stressor, actively engage your prefrontal cortex: do mental math, recall a list, plan your day out loud, or solve a problem. The goal is NOT to suppress the stress response — let your heart rate and adrenaline spike. The goal is to keep your cognitive self online despite the physiological alarm. This is the exercise.

actions.timing: During and immediately after the stressor
actions.details: Use extended-exhale breathing (4 counts in, 8 counts out) during the stressor to modulate heart rate while maintaining cognitive engagement. After the stressor, use physiological sighs (double inhale + long exhale) to actively down-regulate. This teaches rapid recovery — another trainable skill.

benefits: Raises your stress 'ceiling' — the adrenaline level at which cognition fails
Trains prefrontal cortex to stay online during high-arousal states
Builds genuine psychological resilience (not avoidance)
Improves performance in high-stakes situations
Reduces reactivity and emotional hijacking in daily life
Stacks with cold exposure for compounded benefit
science: Stress inoculation works by repeatedly exposing the prefrontal cortex to high-norepinephrine/adrenaline states while requiring it to perform. Over weeks, this raises the arousal threshold at which top-down prefrontal control is lost. Huberman distinguishes this from simply habituating to a stressor — the cognitive engagement during stress is the critical training variable. The protocol is used in military and trauma resilience programs and is grounded in research on prefrontal-amygdala regulation.
contraindications: Not recommended for individuals with PTSD — deliberate stress exposure should be done with professional guidance
Those with cardiovascular conditions should use milder stressors
Do not perform near bedtime — adrenaline will disrupt sleep
Start with short durations and mild stressors; progress gradually over weeks

title: Creativity Enhancement Protocol
description: A two-phase meditation sequence — open monitoring then focused attention — to prime both divergent and convergent thinking, with mood calibration before creative work sessions.

actions.details: Sit comfortably with eyes closed. Let your mind roam freely — don't anchor to any single thought, sensation, or object. If a thought arises, observe it without engaging or suppressing it, then let it pass. The goal is wide, defocused awareness that mirrors the unfocused, associative thinking required for generating novel ideas. This activates the default mode network (DMN), which is where creative connections are made.

Transition to single-point focus — breath, a visual target, or a body sensation. Hold attention on that one point. When your mind wanders, return focus. This transitions you from generative (DMN) mode into evaluative (prefrontal/executive) mode, which is needed for selecting the best idea from what the open monitoring phase generated.

actions.timing: Before the meditation sequence if in a low or neutral mood
actions.details: Creativity requires adequate dopamine tone. If you feel flat or unmotivated, briefly elevate your mood before the sequence: 5 minutes of upbeat music you enjoy, a short social interaction, or 5-10 minutes of light exercise. Dopamine gates creative output via the nigrostriatal pathway — low dopamine produces narrow, uncreative thinking.

benefits: Primes both divergent thinking (idea generation) and convergent thinking (idea selection)
Leverages the default mode network for associative, creative connections
Dopamine optimization supports creative flexibility
Distinct from focus meditation — different goal, different neural circuits
Applicable before writing, problem-solving, design, or strategic planning sessions
science: Creativity requires two distinct neural modes. Divergent thinking (generating many novel ideas) relies on the default mode network (DMN) — the same network active during mind-wandering. Convergent thinking (evaluating and selecting ideas) requires prefrontal executive control. Open monitoring meditation activates DMN; focused attention meditation activates prefrontal circuits. Huberman explains that dopamine, particularly via the nigrostriatal pathway, modulates creative flexibility — low dopamine narrows thinking, adequate dopamine enables broad associative ideation.
contraindications: Do not use immediately after high-intensity exercise (elevated norepinephrine narrows cognitive focus, opposing divergent thinking)
Avoid screens and social media between the two phases — they interrupt the DMN activation

title: Gut Microbiome Support (Fermented Foods)
description: Consume 2-4 servings of low-sugar fermented foods daily to increase gut microbiome diversity and reduce inflammatory markers, as demonstrated in the Stanford study discussed by Huberman.

actions.action: Eat 2-4 servings of fermented foods daily
actions.timing: Spread across meals throughout the day
actions.details: Include low-sugar fermented foods such as: plain yogurt, kefir, sauerkraut, kimchi, kombucha (low sugar), natto, or miso. The key is variety and consistency. Start with 1 serving and increase gradually to avoid GI discomfort. Fermented foods outperformed high-fiber diets for microbiome diversity in the Stanford study.

benefits: Increases gut microbiome diversity (most important metric)
Reduces 19 inflammatory markers (Stanford study finding)
Supports immune system function
May improve mood via gut-brain axis
Better than high-fiber diet alone for microbiome diversity
Easy to incorporate into existing diet
science: A Stanford study by Justin Sonnenburg (discussed extensively on Huberman Lab) compared high-fiber vs. high-fermented-food diets over 10 weeks. The fermented food group showed significantly increased microbiome diversity and reduced 19 inflammatory markers. The fiber group did not show the same diversity improvements, though fiber remains important for existing microbe nourishment.

title: Deliberate Heat Exposure Protocol by Dr. Andrew Huberman
description: A science-backed sauna protocol to enhance cardiovascular health, hormone production, and overall well-being.

actions.details: Use a dry sauna heated to 80–100°C (176–212°F). Start with 5 minutes and gradually increase duration. Aim for 2–3 sessions per week, or up to 7 times per week for optimal cardiovascular benefits.

benefits: Enhances cardiovascular health
Increases growth hormone secretion
Improves mood and reduces stress
Supports longevity and cognitive function

contraindications: Individuals with cardiovascular conditions should consult a healthcare provider before starting any new heat exposure protocols.

title: Neuroplasticity Super Protocol
description: Combine high focus, urgency, acetylcholine, and epinephrine to maximize neuroplasticity during learning sessions. Stack behavioral tools (alertness, focus, repetition) followed by deep rest for consolidation.

actions.action: Generate high alertness before the learning bout
actions.details: Use 1-2 techniques to raise epinephrine/alertness: cold face wash, 25 jumping jacks, cyclic hyperventilation (Wim Hof-style for 25 breaths), or caffeine. You need to feel alert and slightly activated — this releases norepinephrine which flags experiences as important for encoding.

actions.action: Engage in focused, effortful learning for up to 90 minutes
actions.details: Focus intensely on the skill or material you want to learn. Make errors — they signal the nervous system that change is needed. The feeling of strain and frustration is a marker that neuroplasticity is being triggered. Repeat the most difficult elements more often.

actions.action: Perform NSDR or sleep within 1-2 hours after learning
actions.details: Perform a Yoga Nidra / NSDR session or take a nap. Neural replay (consolidation) occurs during states of deep rest and sleep, accelerating the rewiring of circuits that were activated during the learning bout.

benefits: Maximizes rate of neuroplastic change (learning speed)
Applies to motor skills, cognitive skills, and emotional learning
Uses behavioral tools only — no supplements required
Backed by mechanisms of long-term potentiation and depression
NSDR accelerates consolidation without needing full sleep
Framework applicable to any skill at any age
science: Neuroplasticity requires three components: (1) epinephrine/alertness to mark an experience as important, (2) acetylcholine/focus to highlight specific synapses, and (3) rest/sleep for actual rewiring (BDNF-mediated consolidation). The learning happens DURING rest, not during practice. Practice sets the stage; sleep/NSDR completes the rewiring. Huberman calls this the 'neuroplasticity super protocol.'
contraindications: Intense focus sessions can be mentally exhausting — limit to 1-2 per day
Not suitable for casual learning — designed for deliberate skill acquisition
Avoid cyclic hyperventilation if you have respiratory conditions or epilepsy

title: Alpha-GPC Acetylcholine Priming
description: Situational supplementation with Alpha-GPC (300-600mg) 10-20 minutes before demanding cognitive work or training, 3-4x per week, to elevate acetylcholine and sharpen focus and learning.

actions.action: Take Alpha-GPC 10-20 minutes before cognitive work
actions.timing: 10-20 minutes before a focused work session or training
actions.details: Take 300-600mg Alpha-GPC (alpha-glycerophosphocholine) 10-20 minutes before a cognitively demanding session. This is a situational tool — not a daily supplement. Huberman takes it 3-4x per week. It can be stacked with caffeine for a compounded effect. Available in capsule or powder form. Start at 300mg to assess tolerance.

If you prefer food sources, prioritize high-choline foods: 2 egg yolks, 3oz beef liver, or a can of sardines all provide significant choline for acetylcholine synthesis. These are less acute than Alpha-GPC supplementation but support baseline acetylcholine tone.

actions.action: Do not take daily — cycle use
actions.timing: On high-demand workdays or training days only
actions.details: Huberman and research flag a concern with daily choline supplementation: TMAO (trimethylamine N-oxide) production by gut bacteria from chronic high choline intake may increase cardiovascular risk. Keep Alpha-GPC to 3-4x per week, on your most cognitively demanding days. Rest days support acetylcholine receptor sensitivity reset.

benefits: Elevates acetylcholine — the neurotransmitter of focus, attention, and learning
Improves performance on cognitively demanding tasks
Stacks synergistically with caffeine for compounded focus
Supports muscular output when taken before training
Situational — used only on high-demand days, avoiding habituation
science: Acetylcholine is the primary neuromodulator of focused attention and learning. Alpha-GPC is a highly bioavailable choline precursor that crosses the blood-brain barrier and rapidly increases acetylcholine synthesis. Unlike many nootropics, it has direct evidence from human studies for cognitive performance improvement. Huberman discusses it specifically in the context of the Focus Toolkit (Episode 88) as one of the few supplements with a clear, fast-acting mechanism for attention enhancement.
contraindications: Do not take daily — limit to 3-4x per week to reduce TMAO production risk
Those on cholinergic medications (some Alzheimer's drugs) should consult a physician
May intensify vivid dreaming if taken too close to bedtime
Individuals with fish/soy allergies should check the source of their Alpha-GPC product
Not a replacement for sleep — sleep deprivation overrides any supplement-based focus boost

title: Testosterone Optimization (Behavioral Protocol)
description: Behavioral and lifestyle interventions to optimize testosterone levels naturally through sleep, exercise, light exposure, and stress management — no supplements or hormones required.

actions.action: Get bright light exposure early in the day
actions.details: Morning light exposure (especially to the eyes and skin) supports healthy dopamine and luteinizing hormone (LH) signaling, both upstream of testosterone production. This overlaps with the morning sunlight protocol.

Compound movements (squat, deadlift, bench, overhead press) with heavy loads (6-10 rep range) acutely increase testosterone. Multi-joint exercises recruiting large muscle groups produce the largest hormonal response.

Testosterone is primarily produced during sleep (especially REM). Even one week of sleep restriction (5 hours/night) can reduce testosterone by 10-15%. Prioritize consistent sleep timing and duration.

Chronic cortisol elevation directly suppresses gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) and testosterone production. Use breathing techniques, time in nature, social connection, and exercise to manage stress levels.

benefits: Optimizes natural testosterone production
Improves muscle growth, recovery, and strength
Enhances mood, motivation, and cognitive function
Supports bone density and cardiovascular health
No supplements or hormones needed
Benefits general health beyond testosterone
science: Huberman discusses the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis: GnRH from the hypothalamus triggers LH release, which signals the testes (or ovaries) to produce testosterone. Sleep, light exposure, exercise, and stress all modulate this axis. Heavy resistance training acutely elevates testosterone, while chronic stress suppresses it via cortisol-GnRH antagonism.
contraindications: This is not a substitute for medical evaluation of hypogonadism
If experiencing symptoms of low testosterone, get blood work done
Overtraining can paradoxically lower testosterone — rest is essential

title: Sugar Craving Control Protocol
description: Use science-based techniques to reduce sugar cravings by leveraging the gut-brain axis, amino acid supplementation, and behavioral interventions discussed by Huberman.

conditional.question: Are you experiencing sugar cravings today?

actions.action: Use L-glutamine to blunt acute sugar cravings
actions.timing: At the onset of a sugar craving
actions.details: Take 1-2g of L-glutamine (sublingual or in water) when a sugar craving strikes. Glutamine can serve as an alternative fuel source for neurons that are signaling for glucose, reducing the craving within minutes. This is a short-term intervention.

actions.action: Ensure adequate protein and fat at meals
actions.details: Eating protein and healthy fats before carbohydrates blunts blood glucose spikes and reduces subsequent cravings. Aim for 30g+ protein per meal. Starting with protein/fat before starchy carbs improves glycemic control.

actions.timing: Within 30 minutes of finishing a meal
actions.details: Light walking after eating helps clear blood glucose through muscle contraction (GLUT4-mediated uptake), reducing the insulin spike and subsequent crash that drives cravings.

benefits: Reduces sugar cravings through multiple mechanisms
Improves blood glucose stability
Supports healthier food choices long-term
Reduces energy crashes from blood sugar swings
Simple interventions that require minimal effort
science: Sugar cravings are driven by both central (brain dopamine circuits) and peripheral (gut-brain neuropod cell) mechanisms. Huberman explains that neuropod cells in the gut sense sugar and signal the brain via the vagus nerve, creating cravings independent of taste. L-glutamine may blunt cravings by providing an alternative fuel for glucose-sensing neurons. Post-meal walking improves GLUT4-mediated glucose disposal.
contraindications: L-glutamine should be avoided by those with liver disease or kidney disease without medical supervision
Not a substitute for addressing underlying insulin resistance or diabetes
Those with eating disorders should work with a professional

title: Alcohol Harm Reduction Protocol
description: Evidence-based strategies to minimize the negative health effects of alcohol consumption, including gut protection, sleep quality preservation, and hangover mitigation — for those who choose to drink.

conditional.question: Are you planning to drink alcohol today?

actions.action: Eat food (especially protein and fat) before drinking
actions.details: Food in the stomach slows alcohol absorption dramatically. Protein and fats slow gastric emptying the most. Never drink on an empty stomach. This reduces peak blood alcohol concentration and the severity of gut disruption.

actions.action: Hydrate between and after alcoholic drinks
actions.details: Drink water between alcoholic beverages (1:1 ratio ideally). Alcohol is a diuretic that depletes water and electrolytes. Before bed, drink 16-32 oz of water with electrolytes. This mitigates hangover symptoms, most of which are dehydration-mediated.

actions.action: Support gut lining with fermented foods the day after
actions.details: Alcohol disrupts the gut mucosal lining and kills beneficial bacteria. Consuming fermented foods (yogurt, sauerkraut, kimchi) the following day supports gut barrier repair. Consider also supplementing with probiotics.

benefits: Reduces severity of hangovers
Protects gut microbiome from alcohol damage
Minimizes sleep disruption from alcohol
Reduces peak blood alcohol for safer consumption
Practical strategies for those who choose to drink
Supports faster recovery
science: Huberman's episode on alcohol details its effects: alcohol is a toxin metabolized to acetaldehyde (a carcinogen), disrupts gut permeability (leaky gut), suppresses REM sleep, increases cortisol, and depletes folate. While abstinence is ideal for health, harm reduction strategies can meaningfully reduce these effects. Food slows absorption; hydration combats the ADH-suppression diuresis; fermented foods support gut barrier repair.
contraindications: This is NOT encouragement to drink — zero alcohol is the healthiest option
Those with alcohol use disorder should seek professional help, not harm reduction tips
Pregnant women should not consume any alcohol
Those on medications that interact with alcohol should abstain
